CaptureOut.description:
What the server read out of an upload's own metadata, and whether it has read it yet.

`pending` means the read has not happened (the bytes are still arriving, or nothing has asked
yet); `done` is a SETTLED answer even when all three values are null — a file with no capture
date is an answer, not a reason for a composer to keep waiting.
CaptureOut.title: CaptureOut

CreateRacedDetail.description:
Why a keyed create could not be resolved: concurrent writes raced it and the memo they
raced for was deleted before it could be read back. Retrying with the same key is safe — that
is what the key is for — which is why this is a 5xx the client may repeat and not a 4xx
telling it to stop.
CreateRacedDetail.title: CreateRacedDetail

DigestHostingOut.description:
Whether media hosting can work at all, as the panel's status line reads it.

Two independent facts, and the difference between them is the whole value of the endpoint:

* `configured` is the PRESENCE of the three `DROPBOX_*` env keys — never their value, which is
  secret and is echoed nowhere. It answers "could this work?" without touching the network.
* `account` is who those keys actually authenticate as, read live from Dropbox. It is the only
  thing that distinguishes keys that are set from keys that WORK — a rotated refresh token
  leaves `configured` true forever while every upload silently falls back to inline-only.

`account` is null whenever that answer cannot be had — unconfigured, refused, unreachable —
because an admin status line must never be the reason a page 500s.
DigestHostingOut.title: DigestHostingOut

DigestPreviewOut.description:
What a run would send right now, rendered but persisted nowhere.

`html`/`plain` are PART ONE. A preview that concatenated every part would misrepresent the
thing it is previewing — the household receives separate messages — and `parts` says how many
there would be.
DigestPreviewOut.title: DigestPreviewOut

DigestRecipientPatch.description:
Partial by design — the panel toggles `enabled` on its own, without resending the name.

An omitted field is "leave it alone" and is told apart from an explicit `null` (which clears
the display name) by whether the key is present at all, not by the value.
DigestRecipientPatch.title: DigestRecipientPatch

DigestRunClaimOut.description:
The answer to `POST /run`: a run row exists and nothing has executed it yet.

Three fields and no aggregates, because at this instant there are none to report — the row is
the CLAIM, and everything else about it is read back from
`GET /api/admin/digest/runs/{run_id}` (which the response `Location` header names).

`status` is always null here: NULL means "in flight", and a run that already had an outcome
would not be something this endpoint could have just opened.
DigestRunClaimOut.title: DigestRunClaimOut

DigestRunList.description:
One page of runs, in the shape every unbounded list in this API uses (`MemoList`): the
items, the token for the page after, and a total the caller has to ask for.
DigestRunList.title: DigestRunList

DigestSettingsPut.description:
The WHOLE settings row, not a patch.

The panel edits these fields behind one Save bar, so the request that Save
sends IS the new state — which also means a field the client omits is a client bug rather than
"leave it alone", and pydantic says so with a 422. Bounds are plausibility bounds, not policy:
they exist so a typo cannot arm something absurd, and the admin stays free inside them.
DigestSettingsPut.title: DigestSettingsPut

DigestTestSendIn.description:
`{"empty": true}` renders the "no memos selected" body directly, without consulting the
selection at all — the pure SMTP probe, and one that writes no settings anywhere in it.
DigestTestSendIn.title: DigestTestSendIn

DigestVisibilityScope.description: Which memos a digest may mail. `PUBLIC_PROTECTED` is the default.
DigestVisibilityScope.title: DigestVisibilityScope

EditKeyConflictDetail.description:
Why a keyed edit was refused: this owner already used `edit_key` on a DIFFERENT
memo. Both alternatives to refusing are wrong — replaying would answer a PATCH of one memo with
another memo's body (a uid the client never asked about), and applying would leave one key
naming two edits, after which neither could be replayed. `memo_uid` names the memo the key is
bound to so a client can tell a stale key apart from a mis-generated one. Retrying is pointless:
the fix is a fresh key, which is why this is a 4xx and not the 503 a raced edit gets.
EditKeyConflictDetail.title: EditKeyConflictDetail

EditRacedDetail.description:
Why a keyed edit could not be resolved: the write collided on the edit-key
constraint, and the edit it collided with was gone by the time it could be read back — the memo
itself was deleted, taking its recorded edits with it. Retrying with the same key is safe (that
is what the key is for) and self-correcting: the retry finds no memo and answers 404.
EditRacedDetail.title: EditRacedDetail

ExportSettingsPut.description:
The WHOLE settings row, not a patch — the panel saves both profiles behind one Save bar, so
the request IS the new state and an omitted field is a client bug (pydantic answers 422).

Every band here is the vendor-documented envelope, not a plausibility limit, and each is the
exact set the Export panel offers: print quality below 90 shows on gloss paper and above 95
costs bytes for nothing; the print long edge is the measured set of useful rungs (4096 covers a
1.5-page spread of the 21x21 layflat at 300 dpi, 5000 is Blurb's published full-bleed rule,
0 keeps the source's own size); the mail long edge is 2x a 600-800 px rendered width; mail
quality 77-83 is the band mail-client practice puts an inline photo in. The API and the panel
admit exactly the same values, so a request the panel could not have produced is a 422 rather
than a state no UI can show.
ExportSettingsPut.title: ExportSettingsPut

MailSubsampling.description:
Chroma subsampling for the mail profile, in the notation the vendor guidance uses.

`4:2:0` is the mail default and is deliberately NOT what print uses: an inline mail image is
read at a few hundred pixels on a phone, where the halved chroma resolution is invisible and
the bytes it saves are the difference between a message that arrives and one that bounces off
a provider's part cap. `4:4:4` is the only alternative offered — an escape hatch for an image
whose fine coloured detail the subsampling visibly eats. There is no `4:2:2`: it is a
compromise between the two that saves little and is not worth a third answer in a panel.
MailSubsampling.title: MailSubsampling

ManageGrantOut.description:
A step-up grant, returned once and stored only as a hash — like a PAT's plaintext.

`expires_at` is part of the contract rather than a client-side guess: the app has to know when
the management screen it is holding this for goes cold, and the server's deadline is the only
one that decides anything.
ManageGrantOut.title: ManageGrantOut

MapManifest.description:
Which basemap archives are available, and the date of the data they were cut from.

`detail` is null when no region archive has been published; a client renders the world archive
alone rather than nothing at all.

`assets_commit` is the revision of the style's fonts and sprites currently on disk. Unlike an
archive, those files are overwritten IN PLACE at fixed paths when their pin is bumped, so
nothing about their URL would change — and they are served as cacheable for a week. Handing
the client the revision is what lets the style version the URLs it builds, which is the only
thing that can retire a cached copy of the previous ones.

`uncovered` counts the caller's visible pins that fall outside the ground the current detail
archive was cut for — the signal that a re-extract is due, because a detail archive does not
follow the household to a new place on its own. It is null, never zero, when no detail archive
is published or its regions were not recorded: zero would read as full coverage.
MapManifest.title: MapManifest

MapMarker.description:
One located attachment: the feed's ref, plus where and when.

The coordinate lives on THIS model alone. `AttachmentRef` — which every memo body carries —
deliberately does not grow one, so a reader of `/api/memos` learns nothing about where a
photo was taken.
MapMarker.title: MapMarker

MemberOut.description:
One household member, in the field shapes `/api/auth/user` already uses for the caller.

A deliberate subset of `UserOut`: `email` and `role` are the account's own business and no
client needs them to draw a filter row, so they are not published about OTHER people here.
`avatar` is whatever the settings feature stores — a `data:image/…` URL (nothing else is
accepted, capped at 256 KB) or, for an account carried over from old memos, the path string
that came with it — and null for a member who never set one. It is
passed through verbatim rather than normalised, so the value a client renders for a member is
the same one `/api/auth/user` hands that member for themselves.
MemberOut.title: MemberOut

idempotency_key.description: Optional client-generated retry token: a UUID, or any opaque 8-64 character token of [A-Za-z0-9_-], unique per logical create. Posting it a second time returns the memo the first call stored — same uid, same attachments — and returns it with **201, the same status as the original create**. The body is the whole answer (the uid tells a client which memo is now stored), so the status is not used as a second channel, and a safe retry looks exactly like the success it is repeating. Two owners may reuse one token. Without a key, a retry stores a SECOND memo.
idempotency_key.title: Idempotency Key

video_posters.description: Give a video its own poster frame: `{video upload_uid: poster upload_uid}`. The video uid must appear in `upload_uids` (it becomes the attachment); the poster uid must NOT — it is consumed as that video's poster tier and never becomes an attachment of its own, so it stays out of the feed, the library and the export. Without one, the worker picks a hero frame ~12% into the clip, which is the wrong frame for a video that opens on a title card. The poster upload must be a finished JPEG belonging to the caller. Consumed atomically with the memo: if the post fails, both uploads are still there to retry with, and a replayed `idempotency_key` answers with the stored memo without consuming anything a second time.
video_posters.title: Video Posters

edit_key.description: Optional client-generated retry token: a UUID, or any opaque 8-64 character token of [A-Za-z0-9_-], unique per logical edit. Sending it a second time does NOT re-apply the edit; it answers **200 with the memo's CURRENT state** — which is the state after any later write, not a snapshot of what this edit produced. The token records that the edit landed, not what the memo looked like afterwards. Crucially the replay is answered BEFORE `upload_uids` are checked, so a retry whose uploads the first attempt already consumed gets its memo instead of a 409. A key already used on a DIFFERENT memo is refused (409 `edit_key_conflict`); two owners may reuse one token. Without a key, a retried media edit is refused with 409 `uploads_unlinkable`.
edit_key.title: Edit Key

NativeTokenOut.description:
What a device may learn about the credential it is already holding.

No `id`, no stored hash, and never the plaintext: this row is the answer to "how long does
this token have, and when did I last use it", not a second copy of the secret. Withholding the
id also keeps the shape honest: a device acts on no token but the one it presents, so there is
no sibling here to act on and no handle to act with.
NativeTokenOut.title: NativeTokenOut

PhotobookManifestOut.description: The book's manifest: the question that was asked, the tally, and every photo in it.
PhotobookManifestOut.title: PhotobookManifestOut

PhotobookPhotoOut.description:
One photo's page in the book. `width`/`height` are the print rendition's real pixels once it
exists and a projection from the source until then — `projected` says which.
PhotobookPhotoOut.title: PhotobookPhotoOut

PrintMetadataPolicy.description:
What of the source's metadata survives into a print rendition.

`strip` is what the shipped encoder does by writing no EXIF at all. `keep_dates` REBUILDS a
whitelist of date tags into fresh EXIF rather than passing the source's through — a
pass-through would carry GPS coordinates, camera serial numbers and a stale Orientation (which
is already baked into the pixels) into a file that leaves the household for a print service.
Neither policy touches the ICC profile or the baked orientation: those are print correctness,
not metadata.
PrintMetadataPolicy.title: PrintMetadataPolicy

RenditionDetail.description:
One master with its pixel size — the shape the per-photo route returns.

Dimensions are NOT on RenditionItem because they are not in the database: learning them means
opening the file, and RenditionItem rides along on every feed page and library listing. This
subclass exists so the one place that needs them (the print row in the viewer, opened for a
single photo) can pay for them without putting a file read behind the feed.
RenditionDetail.title: RenditionDetail

UploadsUnlinkableDetail.description:
Why a memo write was refused: the requested uploads cannot become attachments.

The two buckets carry different remedies: `missing_upload_uids` (never existed, or expired and
reaped — an upload owned by another user reads as missing too) need a fresh upload;
`incomplete_upload_uids` (fewer bytes received than the declared size) need the transfer
resumed from HEAD.
UploadsUnlinkableDetail.title: UploadsUnlinkableDetail

bearerAuth.description: A personal access token (`memos_pat_…`). Accepted on every /api/* route except /api/pats/*, which takes a browser session or a management grant and never a token, and POST /api/auth/native/exchange, which is anonymous by construction — it is how a device obtains a token in the first place, so requiring one would be circular.

grantAuth.description: A short-lived step-up management grant (`Authorization: Grant …`), obtained from POST /api/auth/native/manage-grant with a handoff code minted by a fresh Authelia login. Accepted only on /api/pats/*, and never mintable from a token — a device PAT manages nothing but itself.

sessionCookie.description: The BFF session cookie set by the OIDC login flow.
sessionCookie.name: memosng_sid

get.description:
Report whether Dropbox hosting is configured, and who the keys authenticate as.

The account lookup is made once per request and only when the keys are present — there is no
process-wide cache, deliberately: a cached identity would keep reporting a working channel
after a token was revoked, which is the exact failure this line exists to expose. It is
read-only (`/2/users/get_current_account`) and answers None on any failure, so a slow or angry
Dropbox costs the panel a null, not an error.

Render what would go out now. Persists nothing and performs NO Dropbox call.

`selected` NAMES the memos rather than counting them: a preview whose answer is a number
cannot be checked against what a run then actually mails.

No request-scoped session is taken. The render walks the filesystem for every card's media,
and the reads it needs are taken in short sessions that close before that walk starts — a
request session would be an idle transaction held across all of it.

schema.title: Response List Digest Recipients Api Admin Digest Recipients Get

post.description:
CLAIM a manual run and answer 202. The worker executes it.

This endpoint commits exactly one thing — the run row, which IS the single-flight lock — and
returns. It does not send, upload or render, and that split is the point: a run can
legitimately last hours (up to `max_memos_per_run` memos, several videos each, Dropbox
upload-session operations that allow 600 s EACH), and a contract that awaited it would tie the
household's mail to a browser tab, a proxy read timeout and a reload. The scheduled run is
already backgrounded for exactly this reason; a manual one is not different work, only
differently triggered.

A manual run sits OUTSIDE the scheduled-day index by design, so it is always possible on a day
that already had one. Its 409 comes from the insert that loses the race for the single-flight
index — never from a pre-flight "is anything running?" read, which would be exactly the TOCTOU
race that index exists to close and which two concurrent callers would both pass.

`Location` names the run, and `GET /api/admin/digest/runs/{run_id}` is where its progress
and its outcome are read back. Until the worker adopts the row it stays `status: null` with no
heartbeat; if no worker ever does, the stale-run sweep closes it as `failed` rather than
leaving it in flight for ever.

Location.description: The claimed run: `GET /api/admin/digest/runs/{run_id}`. Poll it for the run's progress and its terminal status — the work happens in the worker, not in this request.

get.description:
The runs, newest first — the panel's Runs table, paged by keyset.

Unbounded lists in this API page by cursor rather than by a bare `limit`, and this one is
unbounded: a run row is written every day for ever, so a caller that can only ask for "the
first N" can never reach the rest of the history. When more rows follow, `nextCursor` is
non-null; resend it as `?cursor=` for the page after.

Ordered by `started_at` DESC and then `id` DESC: two runs can share a start instant (an
imported row is stamped with the same instant as anything else committed beside it), and an
unstable order would make the table shuffle between refreshes — and would make a keyset cursor
skip or repeat rows, which is worse than shuffling.

`totalCount` is null unless `?with_total=true`, the same opt-in the memo feed uses: a COUNT is
the most expensive part of a page and the table that reads this does not show one.

One run by id — what the `Location` of a 202 from `POST /run` points at.

A claim is only useful if its progress can be read back, and paging the whole list to find one
row is not that.

put.description:
Update the one settings row. There is no create path here, deliberately: the database allows
exactly one row and this router only ever UPDATEs it, so a second one is impossible.

The row is taken FOR UPDATE for the whole request, not because a fresh read is needed but
because arming is a check-then-act: two overlapping requests, one arming the digest and one
disabling the last recipient, would each see the other's pre-state and both pass, leaving an
armed digest with nobody to send to. Disabling a recipient locks that same one row in the same
order, so the two paths serialize against each other and cannot deadlock.

post.description:
Send ONE real mail to the calling admin's own address, and persist nothing.

The destination comes from the authenticated session, never from a request field: an endpoint
that took an address would be an open relay for anyone who reached it, and it would let a probe
mail the configured recipients. It performs no Dropbox upload either — it renders with whatever
hosted links already exist, and a video with none carries the "not hosted" chip.

It stays SYNCHRONOUS, unlike a run, and the reason is that it is bounded by construction: no
uploads, one recipient, one message. Its database reads still happen in short sessions that
close before SMTP is contacted, which is why it takes no request session of its own.

put.description:
Update the one settings row.

The row is taken FOR UPDATE for the whole request. Not for a fresh read: two overlapping saves
would otherwise interleave field by field and commit a profile that is neither of the two the
admins pressed Save on — a mixture of print quality from one and grayscale from the other,
which is a cache key nobody chose. One row, taken in one order by the one writer, so the
second request waits and overwrites a complete state rather than half of one.

get.description:
The household media library the user can see, newest first: their own attachments
(including orphans) PLUS media on any memo visible to them (non-PRIVATE). ?type=image|video
filters by mime prefix; `orphan` flags media not attached to any memo, and `memoUid` names the
memo it does hang on. Another user's PRIVATE or orphan media is excluded — the same visibility
rule the memo surfaces apply. ?order=asc walks the same library oldest-first.

Paged by keyset, like the memo feed: when more rows follow, the response carries an
`X-Next-Cursor` header; resend it as `?cursor=` — with the same filters, which the cursor does
not carry — for the page after. The body is a plain array on every page, cursor or not.

schema.title: Response List Attachments Api Attachments Get

X-Next-Cursor.description: Opaque continuation token — resend it as `?cursor=` (with the same `type`, `limit` and `order`) to get the next page. Absent on the last page.

delete.description:
Delete an attachment — OWNER-only (a mutation, unlike viewing). Removes its media jobs,
DB row, and all on-disk files (original + derived tiers). If it was linked to a memo, the
memo keeps its text; only the media is removed.

post.description:
Attach a print-quality master to an OWNED image attachment (a separate Lightroom print
export). The web rendition keeps displaying; this file is hidden from the feed and
download-only via the `print` tier.

delete.description:
Remove one print master — OWNER-only (a mutation; viewing a master is household-wide). The
screen photo and every derived tier are untouched: only the archive master goes.

get.description:
Download a single print rendition — download-only, household-visible, on the short-session
auth path (never the signed/public fast path; prints are low fan-out, not public-by-uid).

A photo's hidden print renditions, WITH their pixel dimensions (household-visible, like the
legacy print tier). Registered BEFORE the generic /{uid}/{tier} route so the literal
`renditions` segment isn't a tier.

schema.title: Response List Renditions Api Attachments  Uid  Renditions Get

post.description:
Attach — or replace — the print master of an OWNED image, from a finished resumable upload.

Takes an upload_uid rather than a multipart body so a multi-hundred-MB master gets the chunked,
resumable, progress-reporting path every other upload in this app uses.

Trade a handoff code plus its PKCE verifier for a device PAT.

Anonymous by construction — this is how a device gets its first credential, so requiring one
would be circular. It is also cookie-free, which is what keeps CSRF out of the picture: the
request carries no ambient authority a browser could be tricked into attaching.

Only a code minted for the login lane is redeemable here. A management code presented to this
route is refused
like any unknown one (and left unburned): the two lanes ask Authelia for the same thing but buy
very different credentials, and a manage code spent here would hand a year-long device token to
a flow that asked for ten minutes of token management.

Revoke the presenting device token, and only that one.

A bearer may revoke ITSELF and nothing else: the rest of token management takes a browser
session or a step-up management grant obtained through the native login, never a token, so a
leaked device token can neither mint successors that outlive its revocation nor take another
device offline. A session cookie is refused here for the same reason from the other side — the
SPA revokes through `/api/pats/{pat_id}`, which knows which token it is talking about.

Trade a MANAGEMENT handoff code plus its PKCE verifier for a short-lived management grant.

This is the only way a grant comes into existence: the code was
minted by a fresh Authelia authentication minutes ago, and nothing a device already holds can
produce one — a PAT cannot, and neither can an existing browser session. That is the whole
point of a step-up: the capability to mint and revoke this account's tokens is bought with an
authentication, never with a token.

Anonymous by construction, exactly like `/native/exchange`: the code and the verifier ARE the
authority, and the request carries no ambient authority a browser could be tricked into
attaching. A code minted for the login lane is refused here, and that refusal does not burn
it: the purpose is
part of the atomic match, so a code minted for the other lane matches nothing and stays
redeemable on the route it was minted for.

Rotate the presenting device token: mint a successor and revoke the presenter, atomically.

A device token is deliberately bounded — it lives on hardware that gets lost, and nobody
revokes what they have not noticed is gone — which without this route means every phone set up
a year ago signs out one morning with no warning and no way back except a full login. Renewal
refreshes that lifetime from USE instead of removing the bound.

It ROTATES rather than extends: the successor is a new secret and the presenter is gone in the
same statement, so a token copied out of a backup or a log stops working at the owner's next
renewal instead of living the full year twice over.

Restricted to a token that carries an expiry. Nothing marks a device token as one — carrying
an `expires_at` is the only thing that distinguishes it from a token the SPA minted, and only
imperfectly — and only a token that expires can silently sign out, so an unbounded PAT is
refused
(`token_not_renewable`) rather than rotated: token management proper takes a browser session or
a step-up management grant, never the token being presented, and this route reaches no further
than the class it exists for.

Bearer-only, like `native/logout`: the presenting token is the subject of the request, and a
session cookie names no token at all.

get.description:
The presenting device token's own row, and only that one.

A device knows its expiry from the mint response and nowhere else, which means an app that was
reinstalled — or simply restarted after a year — cannot tell the owner how long this phone has
left or when it last spoke. This is the read that closes that, and it reaches no further than
the credential making the request: a leaked token learns nothing it does not already hold, so
the route carries no security decision at all.

Bearer-only, like `native/logout` and `native/renew`. Token management proper takes a browser
session or a step-up management grant — `/api/pats` is where a credential that names another
token lives; a bearer manages nothing but itself.

patch.description:
Rename the presenting device token — the only field of it a device may change.

The name is what the owner reads in the token list, and today it is fixed at the mint from the
device name the app sent; a phone that was renamed, or handed on, keeps the old label forever.

Scoped to the presenting row by the same WHERE the read uses, in ONE statement whose RETURNING
is the response: nothing here can widen to a sibling, and a row that stopped existing between
authentication and the write matches nothing rather than renaming the wrong token.

get.description:
Stream the matching memos as a zip: `<memo-uid>.md` per memo plus a manifest.

With `include_media`, each memo's attachments are carried alongside its text under
`media/<memo-uid>/`, in the rendition the `tier` names (the same tier keys the asset routes
serve). A rendition that isn't on disk is skipped and noted in the manifest.

The photo book for a date range: a print-readiness manifest, or the archive itself.

Selection is the owner's image attachments in memo-date order; `from`/`to` bound the memo date
and are inclusive whole days. `tag` NARROWS that to the memos carrying it — omitting it selects
every image memo in the range, which is what "give me all my photos between two dates" means.

`profile` names the print profile the book is derived at. Omitting it follows this
deployment's export settings, so an admin changing the print profile changes what an export
produces without any client being told; naming one pins the request to it. Two keys are
accepted — the permanent default `print-4096`, whose renditions are the shipped tier, and
whatever the settings currently name; anything else is 422. A non-default profile derives into
its own cache directory, so requesting one never rewrites or invalidates the default tier.

**Requesting a book schedules it.** Both formats enqueue a print rendition for every member
that lacks a current one, so the first request starts the work and later requests report on it;
the enqueue is idempotent, so polling costs nothing.

`format=manifest` (the default) answers with one record per photo — the name it will carry in
the archive, whether its rendition is `ready`/`pending`/`failed`/`unavailable`, its pixel size,
and the **effective dpi** it will print at for the given `page_cm`/`max_pages` geometry, judged
against `dpi`. That is the field worth having: it names the photos a layout program will flag,
before the import rather than after it. Re-fetching it is also how progress is followed.

`format=zip` streams the ready renditions as `0001_<date>_<uid>.jpg`, numbered in book order so
a folder import lands in sequence. Photos that are not ready yet are left out and recorded in
the archive's manifest.json, exactly as the generic export treats a rendition that is missing.

Serve one map style asset — a glyph range or a sprite sheet.

Cached as long as an archive, and for a different reason: these paths ARE rewritten in place
when the assets pin is bumped, so a week of immutable caching is only truthful because the
style asks for them under a URL carrying the revision the manifest reported. A request's query
string is not part of the file lookup; it is the cache key.

List the basemap archives this server currently offers, and how well they cover the pins.

Never cached: it is the pointer that changes when new map data is published, and a client
holding a stale copy would keep asking for an archive that has been superseded.

The ordinary session dependency here, unlike the two routes below: this answer is a few
hundred bytes and the coverage count is a query, so the connection is held for a short
response rather than for a multi-gigabyte transfer. The count itself is cached per viewer for
ten minutes — the manifest is fetched on every map open and every theme toggle.
Every located photo the caller may see, oldest first.

Serve one basemap archive, by byte range.

A map client fetches a few kilobytes per tile out of a multi-gigabyte file, so a ranged request
is the normal case: it answers 206 and states the range it served, a range that starts past the
end of the archive answers 416, and a request without a range header answers the whole file.

head.description:
Serve one basemap archive, by byte range.

A map client fetches a few kilobytes per tile out of a multi-gigabyte file, so a ranged request
is the normal case: it answers 206 and states the range it served, a range that starts past the
end of the archive answers 416, and a request without a range header answers the whole file.

get.description:
Every member of the household, for the client-side "whose memos?" filter.

ASSUMPTION, and the reason this route needs no scoping argument: this is a single-household
instance — every account that exists is a member of the one household, so membership needs
nothing to express it. A multi-tenant deployment would have to record tenancy and filter here;
nothing in this API expresses it today.

Everyone who can authenticate sees the whole roster, and it deliberately does NOT depend on
what the caller can read: a member who has posted nothing, or only PRIVATE memos, still appears
— a filter that silently omitted them would make an empty result indistinguishable from a
member who does not exist, and the roster leaks nothing beyond a display name the household
already sees on every shared memo.

Ordered by (display_name, subject) so the list is stable across calls and across pages of any
client that caches it; `subject` alone breaks the tie for the members with no display name,
whom Postgres would otherwise return in whatever order it liked.

get.description:
What this upload's own metadata says about when it was captured.

NON-CONSUMING and idempotent: it finalizes nothing, deletes nothing and moves nothing, so a
composer may poll it while the person is still typing and then post the memo exactly as it
would have without it. Owner-scoped exactly like every other upload verb, so another owner's
uid answers with the same 404 as one that never existed.

It may still WRITE — once. The first call performs the read the completing append normally
does, for the two cases that append cannot cover: a session that finished before this feature
shipped, and a zero-byte file, which is complete without an append at all. The row lock makes
that exactly-once, and every later poll is a plain read.

Derived tiers only: ?thumbnail=true → thumb, mobile UA → mobile, video → web.
The original path stays 404, as prod is today. Visibility-gated like the memo surfaces:
anonymous callers get derived tiers of PUBLIC memos only, a PAT widens to that user's
visible set, and anything else (private, orphaned, deleted) is 404 — never 403, so the
denial does not disclose that the uid exists.

The privacy policy, served to anyone — no credential, like /health and the association file.

A policy behind a login is not a published policy: App Store review, and any reader deciding
whether to sign in at all, fetch this URL anonymously.
